analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import lower-priced prescription drugs from FDA-approved foreign pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 12 senators including two Republicans, was sent to the Senate health committee and never taken up; it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law so that ordinary people — not just pharmacists and wholesalers — could legally buy FDA-approved prescription drugs from abroad, where the same medicines sell for far less. It would have made the importation program permanent, required all prescription drug packaging to carry counterfeit-resistant security features like those on U.S. currency, and required the Health and Human Services Secretary to write the importation rules within 180 days. The bill never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and the uninsured, who pay the highest drug prices in the world for the same FDA-approved medicines sold cheaper abroad. The bill's own findings state Americans pay up to 1000 percent more than consumers in other countries. Licensed pharmacies and wholesalers already allowed to import would gain a broader legal market.

how_it_helps.text: Allows 'qualifying individuals' — ordinary people, not just pharmacists and wholesalers — to legally import covered prescription drugs, with the HHS Secretary required to write regulations within 180 days of enactment.
Removes the sunset date on the importation provisions, so the program could not lapse under current law's expiration.

Requires all prescription drug packaging to incorporate counterfeit-resistant technologies similar to those the Bureau of Engraving and Printing uses to secure U.S. currency, with counterfeit-resistant packaging standards applied to blister packs, labels, seals, bottles and shipping containers.

Limits eligibility to drugs and manufacturing facilities approved by the FDA and excludes pharmaceutical narcotics, and directs a study comparing misbranded or adulterated shipments from imports with those transported within the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. premium prices would face competition from identical FDA-approved drugs sold at lower prices abroad. Manufacturers would also bear the cost of adding counterfeit-resistant packaging and chain-of-custody procedures, and HHS would bear the cost of writing and enforcing importation regulations.

drawbacks.text: The bill relaxes safety testing for personal imports: authenticity and degradation tests are not required unless the importer is a wholesaler, so an individual's imported drug could enter the country without those checks.

It strips the Secretary's authority to condition importation on a determination that the public is adequately protected from counterfeit or violative products, removing a safety backstop in current law.

The bill's stated savings — citing figures like $635 billion a year in the findings — come from the sponsors' own preamble, not an independent cost estimate in the record, so the size of the benefit to consumers is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the potential upside was large: legal access to the same FDA-approved medicines at the lower prices charged abroad, with an importation program made permanent and packaging security standards added. The cost is borne almost entirely by drug manufacturers, which is why the bill faced an uphill climb. The genuine trade-off is on safety: the bill lightened testing requirements for personal imports and removed the Secretary's discretion to hold back importation if counterfeits could not be kept out, so the design traded some safety oversight for lower prices rather than pairing them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day after it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Byron Dorgan introduced the Pharmaceutical Market Access Act of 2003 on October 23, 2003, joined by 11 original cosponsors including Republicans Olympia Snowe and John McCain and Independent Jim Jeffords.
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, then referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee by unanimous consent on October 24, 2003.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote are recorded, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: U.S. prices, which run far above prices for the same drugs abroad, faced no added competition. American consumers who buy prescription drugs gained nothing.

against.role: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

against.name: Sen. Judd Gregg

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug makers
against.what_they_did: Fought drug reimportation legislation during this period as a threat to U.S. pricing.

sides.party_line_note: Nine of the bill's 12 cosponsors were Democrats, joined by two Republicans (Snowe and McCain) and one Independent; the bill never reached a floor vote, so the full chamber's partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Importation would let Americans buy the same FDA-approved drugs at the far lower prices charged abroad, eroding the premium the U.S. market pays — the bill's findings say Americans pay up to 1000 percent more than consumers in other countries. Manufacturers would also have to add counterfeit-resistant packaging under the bill. Because the bill died in committee, drug makers kept their U.S. pricing intact.

industries.industry: Internet and foreign pharmacies (and U.S. wholesalers)
industries.note: Legal personal importation would create a large new customer base of Americans buying directly, expanding on the market pharmacists and wholesalers already had. Consumers win alongside them, since the pharmacies profit by selling the same drugs for less.
